attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'Won't' is firm language. 'This year' (2025) is kept as the horizon. The proposition covers only the reliability part, which is right.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: agents fail a large share of realistic tasks, so they can't be trusted unsupervised. A bar of around 90% with no threshold given is reasonable. Reading 'demos' as agents generally shown in 2025 is not stretched.

evidence.note: Sep 2025 revision of TheAgentCompany: the best agent completes 30% of realistic workplace tasks autonomously. This is independent academic evidence.
CRMArena-Pro, May 2025: leading agents reach about 58% single-turn and about 35% multi-turn success. This is research by an industry lab, not a disclosure about its own product.
Company disclosure from Sep 2025: the leading OSWorld score is 61.4%, so about 39% of tasks still fail. It is a self-report, but it cuts against the company's interest on reliability.
SWE-bench Verified at 77.2% is the strongest counterpoint, but it is coding-specific, still under 90%, and a company self-report.

reviews.rationale: The forecast was firm and its 2025 horizon has passed. Independent 2025 benchmarks show leading agents failing large shares of realistic multi-step tasks (30% completion, 35–58% success). Even the best computer-use score was about 61%, and coding reached about 77%, short of the high-reliability bar. This meets the support condition, and the contradiction condition is not met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A claim about what is needed to build agents, restored to the author's wording. Only the typo 'do you what' was fixed. Treating it as causal or necessity is acceptable.

contract.note: The contract rightly reads 'agents' as the reliable, general agents meant in context, and notes that the listed prerequisites have no agreed measures. Treating the claim as untestable is fair.

reviews.rationale: The claim says common sense, theory of mind and the other traits are necessary for agents. None of these has an agreed measure, and no dated event could show they are necessary or not. The claim is not broken, just untestable, so it is not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The garbled 'generative just AI' is reasonably read as generative AI alone. The 'if that's what you want' antecedent and the 'because' explanation are kept.

contract.note: The contract correctly finds no deadline, no measure and no agreed test of the listed capabilities. The claim that generative AI 'isn't the ticket' is open-ended and cannot be settled.

reviews.rationale: The claim is that generative AI alone cannot deliver agents with the listed capabilities. It has no deadline, and the capabilities have no agreed test. The backward-looking part is a broad characterisation. No dated evidence can settle it, so it is not adjudicable.

attribution.note: From the post's own footnote, written by Marcus.

semantics.note: 'Will' is firm. 'Some prompts, some of the time' limits the scope; it is not a hedge on probability. No deadline was given.

contract.note: The plain reading (inconsistent results across runs, strange outputs, hard to predict) matches the words and is ordinary. The early-resolution rule needs both a decline across repeated trials and documented strange behaviour.

evidence.note: τ²-bench, June 2025: leading agents succeed on some runs of the same task and fail on others, and pass^k falls as k increases. This shows inconsistency.

Anthropic's Project Vend report, published June 2025, on events in Mar–Apr 2025: the agent hallucinated and had an identity episode. It is a company disclosure, but it is a documented experiment and admits the behaviour was unpredictable.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, but the contract's early-resolution rule is met by dated evidence after the post. τ²-bench (June 2025) shows repeated-trial success falling for leading agents, and Project Vend documents strange, unexpected agent behaviour. Both parts hold, and no counterevidence shows consistent behaviour.
